handoff.purpose: Define helper functions and baseline check functions for file write validation.

symbols.name: _module_path
symbols.note: Resolves a dotted module name to a .py file or __init__.py path under root; returns None if neither exists.

symbols.name: _exports
symbols.note: Parses a Python file and returns (frozenset of top-level names, opaque flag). Opaque indicates static reading is not authoritative (star imports or __getattr__).

symbols.name: parses
symbols.note: Checks that proposed content parses as Python. Returns empty string if OK or error message on failure. Skips non-Python files, or if toplevel_defs indicates no change.

symbols.name: not_truncated
symbols.note: Returns error if proposed content is less than min_size_ratio of original size (suspected truncation). Skips for new files or empty original.

symbols.name: no_elision
symbols.note: Returns error if proposed content contains an elision marker (case-insensitive) that was not in the original. Only checks markers in policy.elision_markers.

symbols.name: not_substituted
symbols.note: Partial function (chunk ends before full implementation). Claims to detect file substitution by checking top-level names; only Python files.

claims.text: A Python file that will not parse is not an improvement.
claims.why: The function returns an error message if parsing fails, enforcing that unparseable content is rejected.

claims.text: Runs on CREATED files too, which is where the hole was: an edit that stops parsing was caught by :func:`not_substituted` as a side effect, but a brand-new module that does not parse had nothing looking at it -- the imports check returns early on a parse failure, calling it "a different guard's business". This is that guard.
claims.why: References not_substituted and imports check which are not fully in this chunk; the claim about the hole being filled cannot be verified from this code alone.

claims.text: The classic full-rewrite failure: the model returned part of the file.
claims.why: The function checks if proposed content is too short relative to original, which catches truncation.

claims.text: The model admitting, in prose, that it dropped code. Only NEW markers count. A file that already contained the phrase would otherwise become permanently unwritable by this lane.
claims.why: The function checks that the marker appears in proposed but not in original, so pre-existing markers are ignored.

claims.text: Why this "rewrite" looks like the WRONG FILE, or "" if it looks fine.
claims.why: The function body is truncated; the full logic is not present to verify the claim.

claims.text: MEASURED 2026-07-30, and the reason this exists. A change request naming two files is sent once per file; asked to rewrite ``daedalus/shift.py`` the model returned the contents of ``tests/test_shift.py``. The module was destroyed and the run reported ``status: done``. Three of five multi-file writes failed exactly this way.
claims.why: Historical anecdote; no code in chunk verifies this specific incident.

claims.text: None of the other guards can see it. Truncation compares SIZE, and a substituted file is a perfectly normal size -- the test module was in fact larger than the module it replaced. Elision looks for a model admitting it omitted something, and nothing was omitted: a complete, valid, well-formed file arrived. It was simply the wrong one.
claims.why: Claims about other guards' behavior are not verifiable from this chunk.

claims.text: So this asks the only question that separates the two cases: does the result still contain the thing that was sent? An edit keeps most of a file's top-level names; a substitution keeps none of them.
claims.why: The function implementation is truncated; the specific comparison logic is not fully visible.
